meta.title: Reading the Sky
meta.subtitle: How a single radar sweep turns into tomorrow's forecast
meta.description: An interactive story built with Quantum Maze.

blocks.title: Reading the Sky
blocks.subtitle: Scroll to follow one radar sweep from the antenna to the forecast desk

blocks.text:
Every few minutes a weather radar sends a pulse of energy into the atmosphere and **listens** for the echo. Raindrops, hail and even insects reflect a little of that energy back.

This story walks through what happens next, using *scroll-driven* sections, animated figures and interactive comparisons.

steps.text: **The sweep.** The antenna rotates continuously, tilting upward after each revolution to build a three-dimensional volume.
**The ground.** Terrain and buildings also return echoes. These *clutter* signals must be filtered before rain can be measured.
**The product.** After filtering and calibration, the echoes become a map of rainfall intensity that forecasters can read at a glance.

blocks.caption: Drag the handle to compare a coarse product with an enhanced one.

blocks.text: A forecast is only as good as the observations that feed it.

items.title: Pulse transmitted
items.text: A short burst of microwave energy leaves the antenna.

items.title: Echo received
items.text: Reflections return from targets up to a few hundred kilometres away.

items.title: Volume complete
items.text: All elevation angles are scanned and products are generated.

items.title: Forecast updated
items.text: Nowcasting systems extrapolate the motion of storm cells.

points.title: Valley
points.text: Low terrain can be hidden behind ridges — a beam blockage zone.

points.title: Ridge line
points.text: A source of ground clutter at the lowest elevation angle.

items.title: Reflectivity
items.text: How much energy comes back — related to rain intensity.

items.title: Velocity
items.text: Doppler shift reveals motion toward or away from the radar.

items.title: Polarimetry
items.text: Horizontal vs vertical pulses distinguish rain, hail and snow.

blocks.question: Why does the radar tilt upward after each rotation?
options: To scan a full 3-D volume of the atmosphere
blocks.explanation: Stacking several elevation angles builds a three-dimensional picture of storms.
